newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris setback underlines right's election defeat.
newsitem.headline: Paris setback underlines right's election defeat.

text.p: The French right lost its lock on Paris on Sunday in a setback mirroring its nationwide defeat in a parliamentary election and undoing years of work by former mayor Jacques Chirac to make the capital a rightist stronghold.
The left, which had held two of the capital's 21 districts, won seven more in Sunday's poll, including three seized from members of now-President Chirac's centre-right cabinet.
But current mayor Jean Tiberi, who took over at city hall two years ago when his Gaullist mentor Chirac became president, kept his seat despite being the target of a sleaze probe.
"I am particularly pleased because I have been the victim over the past several months of unspeakable calumnies," Tiberi told reporters following official word he had won re-election.
"The voters ... who have known me for a long time have once again recognised my integrity by placing their confidence in me, and I sincerely thank them," he said.
Tiberi, a member of parliament since 1968, is under judicial investigation over alleged payment of a fictitious salary to his wife Xaviere by a Gaullist-run local authority in the Paris region.

Tiberi was also president of the Paris housing authority at a time when the Gaullist RPR allegedly received illicit funding through kickbacks on public housing contracts, according to another judicial probe.
Reflecting his constituents' anger, 28 people had run against Tiberi in his Left Bank district.

Among the rightist losers in Paris in Sunday's poll were Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, Employment Minister Anne-Marie Couderc, Environment Minister Corinne Lepage and Patrick Stefanini, a former senior aide to outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

The handwriting had been on the wall for the right since 1995, when Socialists captured six of the capital's 20 municipal districts in city council elections following a series of housing scandals which became known as "Chirac-town".
Chirac, who ruled over Paris for nearly 18 years until he was elected president in May 1995, had won a "grand slam" of all 20 districts in the previous two municipal elections in 1983 and 1989.

The city had been rocked by disclosures that dozens of Chirac's political cronies, including outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe, several of his relatives and Tiberi's two children lived in low-rent apartments belonging to the city, along with numerous senior civil servants, other bigwigs and journalists.
Tiberi later announced he would auction off 1,000 or more of the city-owned apartments that were at the heart of the outcry. None of them has yet been sold.
